title: More on why I don’t like John Doyle’s work: @Joe Weinberg #theatre #a...
transcript: Another day, another crusty theatre artist whining about trigger warnings instead of making interesting art. And let me tell you, I’ve made videos like this before about artists I actually like, so I could not be more delighted to make another one about one of my least favorite directors, John Doyle. These sentiments seem to be very common in the old guard of theatre. And not only is it a blatant unwillingness to understand the legitimate mental health concerns that prompted the creation of content warnings in the first place, they also keep trotting out this tired old argument about “theatre is meant to upset you. It's meant to make you afraid.” And like, first of all, this feels like a wildly oversimplified, almost childish view of the purpose, the benefits, and the range of storytelling opportunities in live theatre. All these grown-@ss theatre artists sound like a bunch of college freshmen who just found out that you could say curse words in theatre. And now this attempt to be “edgy” becomes their entire metric for how to make compelling art. Also, like, I would be slightly more sympathetic to this line of thinking if this was coming from like 2013 or 2014 when conversations like this were kind of just getting traction, when they could be more afraid of the consequences that might come, and maybe there even was more of a balance to be struck. But it's 2026 folks! Not only are content warnings more unobtrusive than ever — they're easy to access if you want them, but easy to avoid if you don't want them — But also, no one's really getting outraged by sensitive content in theatre except when it's poorly executed. They keep whining about “Shakespeare wasn't afraid of violence,” “the Greeks weren't afraid of violence.” Well, guess what? No one stopped doing Shakespeare. No one stopped doing the Greeks. This is a made up problem that they can't stop complaining about. Meanwhile, this is real rich coming from John Doyle of all people, a director who, for the last decade or so, has been churning out some of the most boring, lifeless theatre i've ever seen. He talks about “challenging” the audience, meanwhile the most challenging thing about his productions is staying awake.
